prompt: A request reaches `/orders/1` with no token at all. Which status does the bookshop answer, and which question failed?
hint: Who is asking comes before what they may do.

choices.text: 403, because the request is not authorised
choices.why: A 403 needs somebody to refuse: the server would have to know who is asking and decide that person may not. With no token, it never learns who is asking.

choices.text: 401, because authentication failed
choices.why: Right. Nobody is identified, so authentication fails first, and HTTP calls that 401 Unauthorized even though it means "not authenticated".

choices.text: 404, because the order cannot be found without a customer
choices.why: The order lookup lives in the controller, and this request never gets that far: the filter chain answers before Spring MVC sees it.

choices.text: 400, because a required header is missing
choices.why: A missing Authorization header is not a malformed request; it is an unauthenticated one, and the answer names the scheme it expects.

prompt: The 401 and 403 answers in this lesson have an empty body, while a missing order comes back as `application/problem+json` from lesson 7's `ApiErrorHandler`. Why the difference?
hint: Where in the request's path does each answer come from?

choices.text: Spring Security forbids a body on a 401 or a 403
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; an entry point or an access-denied handler on the chain can write any body. The bookshop simply has not configured one.

choices.text: The error handler skips responses whose status is below 404
choices.why: A @RestControllerAdvice is chosen by exception type, not by status, and it handles 400s from validation in this very application.

choices.text: A filter answers before the DispatcherServlet, so no advice runs
choices.why: Right. A @RestControllerAdvice belongs to Spring MVC, and a request refused by the filter chain never reaches Spring MVC.

choices.text: Security failures are written to the log instead of being returned to the client
choices.why: They are returned, with a status and a WWW-Authenticate header; only the body is empty.

prompt: A request for `/auth/token` arrives with a valid bearer token and no password. What happens?
hint: `FilterChainProxy` hands each request to one chain.

choices.text: Chain 1 fails, so chain 2 accepts the token and lets it through
choices.why: There is no second try: the first chain whose matcher matches owns the request, whether it passes or not.

choices.text: Only chain 1 runs, finds no Basic credentials: 401
choices.why: Right. Chain 1 owns /auth/token and knows HTTP Basic, not bearer tokens, so the token is ignored and the request is unauthenticated.

choices.text: Both chains run, and the request needs to pass both
choices.why: Chains are alternatives, not layers. Every filter that runs belongs to the one chain that matched.

choices.text: A new token is issued, since the old one proves who is asking
choices.why: TokenController only runs after Basic authentication succeeds, and a bearer token is not Basic.

prompt: Match each piece of the bookshop's security to its job.
hint: The figure of the two chains.

pairs.right: hands the request to the first chain that matches
checks a user name and password on /auth/token
checks the signature and expiry of a JWT
applies the rules such as hasAuthority

right_distractors: turns an exception into a problem detail

prompt: Why does the bookshop store a bcrypt hash of each password rather than the password encrypted with a key?
hint: What does the server ever need to do with a stored password?

choices.text: Encryption is too slow to run on every login request
choices.why: Speed is the wrong axis: bcrypt is the slower of the two, on purpose.

choices.text: Java has no built-in encryption
choices.why: The JDK has had javax.crypto for decades. The choice is about what a server should be able to do, not what it can.

choices.text: Only checking is needed, and a hash is one-way
choices.why: Right. Whatever the server can decrypt, whoever copies its data and key can decrypt too; a one-way hash leaves nothing to decrypt.

choices.text: A hash is shorter, which saves space in the table
choices.why: Both are short strings; a bcrypt hash is 60 characters. Size is not what is being protected.

prompt: `HashPassword` hashed `ana-reads-books` twice and printed two different strings, and both checked. How can both be right?
hint: Look at the 22 characters after `$2a$10$`.

choices.text: bcrypt mixes the current time into the hash it computes for the password
choices.why: No clock is involved; a hash from another day, the stored one, also checked.

choices.text: `matches` ignores the last characters of the hash
choices.why: It compares the whole computed hash; change one character of a stored hash and it no longer matches.

choices.text: The two are encryptions of the password under two different keys
choices.why: There is no key and nothing is decrypted; the hash is one-way.

choices.text: Each hash carries its own random salt, which `matches` reads back
choices.why: Right. The salt is stored inside the hash, so checking needs nothing else, and the same password never gives the same hash twice.

prompt: A bcrypt hash with cost `10` takes some time to check. Raised to cost `12`, how much longer does each check take?
hint: The cost is an exponent.

choices.text: 20% longer, since 12 is 20% more than 10
choices.why: That reads the cost as a count of rounds. It is the exponent of the count: 2 to the 10th against 2 to the 12th.

choices.text: Twice as long
choices.why: One step of cost doubles the work; this is two steps.

choices.text: Four times as long
choices.why: Right. Each step of cost doubles the work, so two steps multiply it by four, for the server and for anybody guessing against a stolen table alike.

choices.text: A hundred times as long
choices.why: That would be about seven steps of doubling, not two.

prompt: What is the `{bcrypt}` at the front of a stored password for?
hint: The encoder in `SecurityConfig` is a delegating one.

choices.text: It tells the delegating encoder which algorithm made the hash, so old and new algorithms can sit in one table
choices.why: Right. A system can store {argon2} hashes for new passwords while every {bcrypt} hash keeps checking.

choices.text: It is part of bcrypt's own format, like `$2a$`
choices.why: bcrypt's format starts at $2a$. The braces are Spring's label, read and removed before bcrypt sees the hash.

choices.text: It marks the password as encrypted rather than plain
choices.why: Nothing here is encrypted; the prefix names a hashing algorithm, and {noop} is the one that would mean plain text.

choices.text: It sets the cost factor to the default
choices.why: The cost is the 10 inside the hash itself.

prompt: With HS256, what does the server do with `BOOKSHOP_JWT_SECRET`?
hint: HMAC is a keyed hash.

choices.text: Encrypts the payload so that only the server can read it
choices.why: HS256 signs; it does not encrypt. The payload decoded with basenc in plain sight.

choices.text: Signs each token and checks each signature with it
choices.why: Right. HMAC is symmetric: the one secret makes the signature and verifies it, which is why it must never leave the server.

choices.text: Hashes the users' passwords with it
choices.why: Passwords are hashed by bcrypt with a salt per hash; the JWT secret plays no part.

choices.text: Sends it to the client with the first token
choices.why: A client holding the secret could sign any token it liked, with any scope.

prompt: Started without `BOOKSHOP_JWT_SECRET` in the environment, the bookshop refused to start, and the value it complained about was `"${BOOKSHOP_JWT_SECRET}"`. What saved it?
hint: Count the characters of the placeholder.

choices.text: Spring refuses any placeholder it cannot resolve to a value
choices.why: Not here: it bound the placeholder text as the value. Had that text been long enough, nothing would have complained.

choices.text: @Size(min = 32) refused the 22-character placeholder
choices.why: Right. Bean Validation on the properties record was the only check, and without it the shop would sign tokens with a key printed in the lesson.

choices.text: NimbusJwtEncoder rejected the key when the bean was built
choices.why: The failure report names the binding of JwtProperties, before any encoder exists.

choices.text: The database refused the connection without a secret being set
choices.why: The database password is a separate property, and it was set.

prompt: In a decoded payload, the claim that names whose token it is is `___`.
hint: Three letters, short for "subject".

prompt: A colleague proposes putting each customer's e-mail address and delivery address in the token, "to save a database query". What is wrong with that?
hint: Who can read a payload?

choices.text: A JWT cannot carry claims other than iss, sub, iat, exp and scope
choices.why: A JWT may carry any claims; scope itself is one the bookshop chose.

choices.text: The HMAC signature would no longer fit in its 32 bytes
choices.why: An HMAC-SHA256 signature is 32 bytes whatever the length of what it signs.

choices.text: Anybody holding the token can read the payload
choices.why: Right. base64url is readable by anybody with basenc, including whoever finds a token in a log or a copied header.

choices.text: The server could not verify a token that long
choices.why: Length does not stop verification; it makes every request heavier, which is a smaller problem than the exposure.

prompt: The forged token kept ana's original header and signature and changed only the payload's scope. Which check refused it, and why could ana not repair the signature herself?
hint: What is the signature computed over, and with what?

choices.text: The expiry check; editing a payload resets its exp
choices.why: exp was copied unchanged and still lay in the future. The failure was about the signature.

choices.text: The scope check; catalogue:write is reserved for the clerk's user name
choices.why: Authorisation never ran. The token was refused before any rule was read, with 401 rather than 403.

choices.text: The signature check, since the HMAC over the new payload differs and computing a new one needs the server's secret
choices.why: Right. Anybody can recompute the base64url, but nobody without the secret can produce the 32 bytes that match it.

choices.text: The decoder, because base64url without padding is malformed
choices.why: Unpadded base64url is how every JWT is written, ana's genuine one included.

prompt: Ana's token carries `"scope":"orders"`. Which authority does the bearer filter give the request?
hint: A prefix is added.

choices.text: `orders`
choices.why: That is the authority in the user list. From a token, every scope gets a prefix, so a rule naming plain orders would match nothing.

choices.text: `SCOPE_orders`
choices.why: Right, and that is the name the rules in apiChain are written against.

choices.text: `ROLE_orders`
choices.why: ROLE_ is the prefix hasRole adds, for roles; scopes from a JWT get SCOPE_.

choices.text: `FACTOR_PASSWORD orders`
choices.why: That is what the scope claim would hold if TokenController did not filter FACTOR_ out, and it is not an authority name.

prompt: Which of these requests succeed with ana's token? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the rules table from the top.

choices.text: `GET /books/1`
choices.why: Right. permitAll lets it through with or without a token.

choices.text: `POST /orders` with one line
choices.why: Right. SCOPE_orders is the authority the rule asks for, and ana has it.

choices.text: `POST /books` with a valid new book
choices.why: That rule asks for SCOPE_catalogue:write, which only the clerk's token carries: 403.

choices.text: `GET /orders/1` for an order the clerk placed
choices.why: The scope rule lets it in, and then OrderService finds the order is not ana's: 404.

prompt: Without its `FACTOR_` filter, `TokenController` wrote `"scope":"FACTOR_PASSWORD orders"`. Why is it better left out of the token?
hint: What does FACTOR_PASSWORD describe, and when?

choices.text: It makes the token too long to be signed with HS256 at all
choices.why: HS256 signs input of any length; a few more characters change nothing.

choices.text: It would quietly give the token access to every single endpoint
choices.why: No rule names it, so it grants nothing. The trouble is what it claims, not what it opens.

choices.text: It says how ana signed in, not what the token allows
choices.why: Right. In the token it would become SCOPE_FACTOR_PASSWORD on every request, a word that reads like a permission and that no rule checks.

choices.text: It reveals the user's password to whoever reads the payload
choices.why: It names the kind of factor, password, and nothing about the password itself.

prompt: Somebody adds `.requestMatchers("/orders/**").authenticated()` to `apiChain`, directly above the `SCOPE_orders` rule. A token whose scope is only `catalogue:write` then asks for `GET /orders/1`. What happens at the door?
hint: Which rule decides?

choices.text: It gets through, because the new rule matches first
choices.why: Right. The first matching rule decides, so the narrower SCOPE_orders rule below it is never read for that path.

choices.text: 403, because both rules must pass and SCOPE_orders is missing
choices.why: Rules are not combined; one decides. That is why the order they are written in matters.

choices.text: Spring refuses to start, since two rules name one and the same path
choices.why: Two matchers for one path are allowed. What Spring refuses at start-up is a rule written after anyRequest().

choices.text: 401, because the token's scope does not match the path
choices.why: 401 is about who is asking, and the token is valid; a scope can only ever lead to a 403.

prompt: Why is `csrf.disable()` correct for the bookshop as it stands?
hint: What does a browser attach to a request by itself?

choices.text: An API that answers in JSON cannot be the target of a CSRF attack at all
choices.why: CSRF is about how the request is authenticated, not about the format of the answer. A JSON API signed in by cookie is a target.

choices.text: HTTPS already prevents cross-site requests
choices.why: HTTPS protects the request in transit; a forged request from another site travels over HTTPS just as well.

choices.text: Nothing authenticates by cookie, and browsers never add Authorization
choices.why: Right. A forged request from another site arrives with no credentials and gets 401, so there is nothing for a CSRF token to protect.

choices.text: The bearer filter checks every request's Origin header
choices.why: No filter in either chain looks at Origin; the protection comes from where the credential travels.

prompt: A front-end team asks for the JWT to be set as an `HttpOnly` cookie instead of being kept by their JavaScript. If the bookshop agrees, what else must change?
hint: Re-read the condition under which CSRF was turned off.

choices.text: Nothing, since the token is still signed
choices.why: The signature proves the token is genuine. CSRF is a genuine token sent by the victim's own browser.

choices.text: CSRF protection has to come back on, since a browser will now send the credential with any request to the site
choices.why: Right. The moment a cookie authenticates, a page on another site can make the browser send it, which is exactly what CSRF protection exists for.

choices.text: The session policy must become IF_REQUIRED
choices.why: A cookie holding a JWT is still stateless on the server; no HttpSession is involved.

choices.text: The token's lifetime must drop to two seconds
choices.why: Lifetime limits a stolen token; it does nothing about a forged request sent within that lifetime.

prompt: Ana reports that her laptop was stolen ten minutes after she fetched a token. What can the bookshop, as written, do about that one token right now?
hint: What does the server remember about the tokens it issued?

choices.text: Delete ana's session, which ends the token
choices.why: Both chains are stateless; there is no session to delete.

choices.text: Change ana's password, which invalidates her tokens
choices.why: The password is checked only at /auth/token. A token already issued never meets it again.

choices.text: Add the token to a revocation list that the filter already reads
choices.why: That list does not exist here. It can be built, with a jti claim, and it brings back state on the server.

choices.text: Change the secret, ending all tokens, or wait for exp
choices.why: Right. The server holds nothing to cross out; a new secret ends every token at once, and the fifteen-minute lifetime ends this one soon.

prompt: A token with a two-second lifetime was still accepted five seconds after it was issued. How many seconds of clock skew does Spring Security's decoder allow past `exp` by default?
hint: It was refused after sleeping a further minute.

prompt: Where does the customer of a new order come from now?
hint: The client can no longer write it.

choices.text: The `customer` field of the request body
choices.why: That component was removed from OrderRequest; a customer field sent anyway is ignored.

choices.text: The `sub` claim of the token the bearer filter verified
choices.why: Right. The controller reads it with @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt and getSubject(), from a token the server signed itself.

choices.text: The user name in an HTTP Basic header sent with the order
choices.why: Basic is accepted only on /auth/token; the order request carries a bearer token.

choices.text: A session attribute set when ana signed in
choices.why: There is no session; each request proves itself with its own token.

prompt: The clerk asks for ana's order 1 and gets the same 404 as for order 99, which does not exist. Why not answer 403?
hint: What would a 403 tell somebody counting up ids?

choices.text: 403 is reserved for answers from the filter chain
choices.why: A controller or an exception handler may answer 403 too. The choice here is about what the answer reveals.

choices.text: A 403 would confirm that the order exists
choices.why: Right. 404 says nothing about whether the order exists, which is all a stranger should learn.

choices.text: The clerk holds SCOPE_orders, so a 403 would be wrong here
choices.why: The scope only got the request past the door. Ownership is a separate check, and refusing on it could have been either code.

choices.text: OrderNotFoundException is the only exception the handler maps
choices.why: ApiErrorHandler maps several exceptions; one for "not yours" could be added. The service throws not-found on purpose.

prompt: Ana sent `{"customer":"clerk", "lines":[...]}` with her token, and the order came back with `"customer":"ana"` and status 201. What happened to the `customer` property?
hint: Compare the JSON with the record it is read into.

choices.text: The service compared it with the token and corrected it
choices.why: The service never sees it: place takes the customer from the controller, which takes it from the token.

choices.text: Bean Validation removed it as invalid
choices.why: Validation checks the components a record has; it does not remove properties, and a failure would have been a 400.

choices.text: OrderRequest has no such component, and Spring Boot's Jackson ignores a property the record lacks
choices.why: Right. The field the client could forge no longer exists, so sending it changes nothing.

choices.text: The scope rule stripped it, since ana lacks catalogue:write
choices.why: Authorisation rules look at the path and the authorities, never inside the body.

prompt: Put in order what happens when ana's `POST /orders` with a bearer token is accepted.
hint: Filters first, Spring MVC last.
items: FilterChainProxy hands the request to chain 2
The bearer filter checks the signature and exp
The scope claim becomes the authority SCOPE_orders
AuthorizationFilter finds the rule for /orders satisfied
OrderController reads the subject and the service saves the order
trap: Authorisation cannot come before the token is checked: until then there are no authorities to compare.

prompt: Match each request to the status the bookshop answers.
hint: One of them never reaches a controller and one never reaches a rule.

pairs.left: GET /orders/1 with a token whose payload was edited
GET /orders/1 for ana's order with the clerk's token

prompt: The bookshop is run as two instances behind a load balancer, each started after its own `export BOOKSHOP_JWT_SECRET=$(openssl rand -base64 32)`. What do clients see?
hint: Which secret checks a token that the other instance signed?

choices.text: Nothing unusual, since the tokens are stateless
choices.why: Stateless means no session is shared, which helps; it still needs the one secret shared, and here it is not.

choices.text: 403 on every request routed to the second instance
choices.why: A signature that does not verify is an authentication failure, so the answer is 401, not 403.

choices.text: A 401 whenever a request reaches the other instance
choices.why: Right. Each instance checks with its own secret, so a token is good on one and invalid on the other; one shared secret fixes it.

choices.text: A JSESSIONID mismatch error raised by the load balancer itself
choices.why: Neither chain creates a session, so there is no JSESSIONID to mismatch.

prompt: A new endpoint, `DELETE /books/{id}`, is added to `BookController`, and nobody touches `SecurityConfig`. Who can call it?
hint: Walk the rules from the top with the method and the path.

choices.text: Nobody, because no rule names DELETE
choices.why: A request no other rule matches falls to anyRequest(), which does not refuse everybody.

choices.text: Everybody, because /books/** is permitted
choices.why: That permitAll is for GET only; a DELETE does not match it.

choices.text: Anybody with a valid token, ana included, since only anyRequest().authenticated() matches it
choices.why: Right. The default for an unlisted request is "any signed-in user", so a destructive endpoint needs its own rule, such as SCOPE_catalogue:write.

choices.text: Only the clerk, because POST /books needs SCOPE_catalogue:write
choices.why: Rules match a method and a path; the POST rule says nothing about DELETE.
